title: Optimal Pairs Are Exactly Saddle Points
body_html:
Optimal Pairs Are Exactly Saddle Points

For a finite matrix game $A$, the product $X(A)\times Y(A)$ of optimal-strategy sets is exactly the set of saddle points of $A$.
proof_html:
Let $v=\operatorname{val}(A)$. If $x\in X(A)$ and $y\in Y(A)$, then $xAy'\ge v$ for every mixed column $y'$ and $x'Ay\le v$ for every mixed row $x'$. Applying these inequalities to $y$ and $x$ gives $xAy=v$, so $$ x'Ay\le xAy\le xAy' $$ for all $x'$ and $y'$. Thus $(x,y)$ is a saddle point. Conversely, if $(x,y)$ is a saddle point, then $$ x'Ay\le xAy\le xAy' $$ for all $x'$ and $y'$. Therefore $x$ guarantees at least $xAy$ and $y$ holds player $1$ to at most $xAy$. Weak duality forces this common bound to be the value, so $x\in X(A)$ and $y\in Y(A)$.

References

  • [MFoGT, Prop. 2.4.1(d)] Laraki, Renault, and Sorin, Mathematical Foundations of Game Theory, references/MechDesign.pdf. X(A) x Y(A) is the set of saddle points.
